name: Taban
bio: The book describes Taban of Delhi as famous for his beauty as for his poetic talent, a pupil of Hatim and a friend of Mazhar and Sauda, descended from the Prophet on both his father’s and mother’s side.

The 2 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poems.title: Repent not, for repentance is in vain
poems.author: Taban
poems.translator: trans. Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1919)
poems.text:
Repent not, for repentance is in vain,
    And what is done is done;
What shouldst thou reck of me and all my pain?
    For what is done is done.

They said to her--Behold him, he is dead!
    How did he lose his life, unhappy one?
--O bury him deep in the grave, she said,
    For what is done is done.

This is the pain of love that I have caught,
    And what is done is done;
A thousand remedies avail me naught,
    And what is done is done.

For love I gave the honour of my name,
    And Good and Evil are to me as one;
Let all the world chastise me with its blame,
    For what is done is done.

The dust of Taban we could find no more,
    But yet nor rest nor respite hath he won;
His breath, his soul, floats round thee as before,
    And--what is done is done.

poems.title: I longed that the Beloved might come to me
poems.author: Taban
poems.translator: trans. Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1919)
poems.text:
I longed that the Beloved might come to me,
Or Patience come and in my heart remain;
But neither came, and now at last I see
The only constant friend I have is Pain.
